intro.title:
Notification system
OTP, campaigns, DLQ
intro.subtitle: One event in, millions of messages out: outbox, priority topics, idempotent workers and a dead-letter queue you can replay.

cues.cap: Designing a notification system: push, email and SMS at scale, scenario by scenario.
cues.say: Designing a notification system: push, email and S M S at scale, scenario by scenario.

cues.cap: The transport is the easy part. The hard parts: never lose a message, never send it twice, keep a two-million-person campaign from blocking a login code, and replay failures safely.

scenes.title: Eight services, one durable log, three paths

steps.cap: The write is synchronous and tiny: a product calls Public API over HTTPS, the API stores the alert and an outbox row in one Postgres transaction and returns 202.
steps.title: Write path
steps.note: The caller waits milliseconds. Nothing is sent yet, but nothing can be lost: the alert and the event are one atomic write.

steps.cap: Everything else is asynchronous: Outbox Relayer moves rows into Kafka, Fan-out Step expands events into batches with preferences, dedup and templates, and per-channel Notification Workers call the providers.
steps.title: Transport path
steps.note: Two backpressure points: the relayer reads as a stream, and the Fan-out consumer regulates with batch size and pause() / resume().

steps.cap: Providers answer later through webhooks into Delivery Status Consumer, and everything that fails ends up in a dead-letter queue that Admin Service can replay.
steps.title: Delivery, status, failures
steps.note: Incoming webhook traffic is about the same size as outgoing sends, and the DLQ is a daily volume, not an exception.

scenes.title: A login code, from 202 to DELIVERED

steps.cap: A user logs in. The product's auth service calls POST /notifications with event type otp, the recipient and the code.
steps.say: A user logs in. The product's auth service calls post slash notifications with event type O T P, the recipient and the code.
steps.note: Products publish events, not messages. The notification system decides channel, text and timing.

steps.cap: Public API validates the event and, in a single SQL transaction, inserts the alert and an outbox row. It returns 202 in milliseconds: nothing is sent yet, but nothing can be lost.
steps.say: Public A P I validates the event and, in a single S Q L transaction, inserts the alert and an outbox row. It returns two-oh-two in milliseconds: nothing is sent yet, but nothing can be lost.
steps.note: Writing to Postgres and then to Kafka are two operations; a crash between them would lose the alert. The outbox makes them one.

steps.cap: Outbox Relayer streams the new row with pg-query-stream, or Debezium reads it from the WAL, and publishes it to notifications-critical: a separate topic from marketing, with its own workers and its own provider quota.
steps.say: Outbox Relayer streams the new row with P G query stream, or Debezium reads it from the write-ahead log, and publishes it to notifications critical: a separate topic from marketing, with its own workers and its own provider quota.
steps.code:
SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL
→ produce notifications-critical
  { event_id: 'evt_91', type: 'otp', user: 'u42' }
→ UPDATE outbox SET published_at = NOW()
steps.note: Backpressure point 1: the relayer reads as a stream, so a burst of a million rows never fills its memory.

steps.cap: Fan-out Step pulls the message from Kafka. There is one recipient, so it only asks Preference & Rules over gRPC. OTP is transactional: it ignores opt-out and quiet hours and is never throttled.
steps.say: Fan-out Step pulls the message from Kafka. There is one recipient, so it only asks Preference and Rules over G R P C. O T P is transactional: it ignores opt-out and quiet hours and is never throttled.
steps.code:
consume notifications-critical (pull)
→ gRPC Rules.Resolve(user: 'u42', type: 'otp')
← { channel: 'sms', lang: 'bg',
    quiet_hours: ignored, throttle: exempt }
steps.note: Preferences are cached in Redis in front of the Preferences DB, because they are read on every single notification.

steps.cap: It sets a dedup key in Redis with SET NX, so a redelivered event cannot produce a second SMS, and asks Template Service for the text in the user's language.
steps.say: It sets a dedup key in Redis with set N X, so a redelivered event cannot produce a second S M S, and asks Template Service for the text in the user's language.
steps.code:
SET notif:evt_91:u42:sms 1 NX EX 600  → OK
→ gRPC Template.Render('otp', 'bg', { code })
← 'Вашият код за вход е 493 117'
steps.note: Kafka is at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent. Exactly-once does not exist end to end.

steps.cap: The rendered message goes back through Kafka as a batch for the SMS workers. A worker pulls it only when it has a free slot, so a spike waits in the topic instead of crashing the pool.
steps.say: The rendered message goes back through Kafka as a batch for the S M S workers. A worker pulls it only when it has a free slot, so a spike waits in the topic instead of crashing the pool.
steps.title: Fan-out → Kafka → SMS Worker
steps.note: Backpressure point 2: the worker pool scales on consumer lag; the topic absorbs the burst.

steps.cap: The SMS Worker calls Twilio over HTTPS with a dedup key, behind a rate limiter and a circuit breaker. If we retry, Twilio does not send and bill a second SMS.
steps.say: The S M S Worker calls Twilio over H T T P S with a dedup key, behind a rate limiter and a circuit breaker. If we retry, Twilio does not send and bill a second S M S.
steps.note: Failover: a second provider (Vonage) behind the breaker, chosen per country.

steps.cap: On a 2xx the worker records SENT and commits the Kafka offset. A 200 from the provider means 'accepted', not 'the user got it'.
steps.say: On a two x x the worker records sent and commits the Kafka offset. A two hundred from the provider means accepted, not the user got it.
steps.title: Worker → Postgres
steps.code:
UPDATE alerts SET status = 'SENT',
       provider_id = 'SM8f…'
 WHERE id = 'al_91';
commit offset (sms-critical)

steps.cap: Seconds later Twilio calls our webhook with delivered. Delivery Status Consumer checks the signature, answers 200 immediately and stores the event idempotently by provider message id.
steps.say: Seconds later Twilio calls our webhook with delivered. Delivery Status Consumer checks the signature, answers two hundred immediately and stores the event idempotently by provider message I D.
steps.code:
POST /webhooks/twilio
X-Twilio-Signature: …   ✓ verified
{ sid: 'SM8f…', status: 'delivered' }
INSERT INTO delivery_events (sid, status)
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;   → 200
steps.note: Providers resend webhooks too, so this consumer is idempotent by provider_message_id.

steps.cap: Finally it updates the alert to DELIVERED in Postgres. From 202 to DELIVERED should take seconds; the most important alarm in the system is critical-topic lag above thirty seconds.
steps.say: Finally it updates the alert to delivered in Postgres. From two-oh-two to delivered should take seconds; the most important alarm in the system is critical topic lag above thirty seconds.
steps.code:
UPDATE alerts SET status = 'DELIVERED',
       delivered_at = NOW()
 WHERE provider_id = 'SM8f…';

SLO: event → DELIVERED, P99 < 10 s (critical)

scenes.title: A campaign to two million people

steps.cap: Marketing launches 'New course' to every subscriber. That is one event with a recipient rule, not two million requests. The relayer routes it to notifications-bulk.
steps.say: Marketing launches New course to every subscriber. That is one event with a recipient rule, not two million requests. The relayer routes it to notifications bulk.
steps.title: One event, one rule
steps.code:
POST /notifications
{ event_type: 'campaign', template: 'new_course',
  rule: 'subscribers', priority: 'bulk' }
→ outbox → notifications-bulk

steps.cap: Fan-out Step snapshots the subscriber list and splits it into batches of a thousand recipients, each batch a separate Kafka message, so two thousand batches spread across every worker.
steps.title: Fan-out: 2 000 batches
steps.note: The list is a snapshot; someone who unsubscribes a second later is caught by the rules check at send time.

steps.cap: For every recipient it checks preferences: marketing requires consent, quiet hours postpone, throttling folds the 37th notification of the day into a digest; then dedup and template.
steps.say: For every recipient it checks preferences: marketing requires consent, quiet hours postpone, throttling folds the thirty-seventh notification of the day into a digest; then dedup and template.
steps.code:
Rules.Resolve(u, 'campaign')
→ consent? quiet hours (local tz)? sent today < 36?
SET notif:evt_92:u:email 1 NX EX 3600
Template.Render('new_course', lang)
steps.note: Opt-out takes effect immediately, even for messages already queued, because the check happens at send time, not at publish time.

steps.cap: Email workers send through SES with a rate limit; when the provider answers 429 they slow down. The bulk pool never touches the critical quota.
steps.say: Email workers send through S E S with a rate limit; when the provider answers four twenty-nine they slow down. The bulk pool never touches the critical quota.
steps.code:
POST https://email.amazonaws.com/ SendEmail
← 429 Too Many Requests → backoff, slow down
throughput: 3 300 / s at peak

steps.cap: If an OTP arrives meanwhile, it travels on notifications-critical with its own workers and does not wait behind the campaign. In a provider incident, the first action is pausing the bulk consumer group.
steps.say: If an O T P arrives meanwhile, it travels on notifications critical with its own workers and does not wait behind the campaign. In a provider incident, the first action is pausing the bulk consumer group.
steps.title: OTP during the campaign
steps.code:
notifications-critical  lag: 0.4 s   ✓
notifications-bulk      lag: 38 min
incident → pause consumer group 'bulk'
steps.note: A shared topic would put the login code 40 minutes behind the campaign.

steps.cap: Before the real launch the campaign runs in dry-run: fan-out and rules execute fully, but the worker writes to a would_send table instead of calling the provider, so marketing sees the exact count.
steps.title: Dry run and kill switch
steps.code:
mode: dry_run
INSERT INTO would_send (event, user_id, channel)
→ 1 937 412 rows, 0 provider calls

kill switch: campaign.cancelled → workers skip

steps.cap: SendGrid returns 503 for an email. The worker does not block the partition by waiting: it publishes the message to notifications-retry with a next attempt time and commits the offset.
steps.say: SendGrid returns five-oh-three for an email. The worker does not block the partition by waiting: it publishes the message to notifications retry with a next attempt time and commits the offset.
steps.title: Transient error
steps.code:
POST SendGrid /v3/mail/send → 503
→ produce notifications-retry
  { ..., attempt: 1, next_attempt_at: now + 2 s }
commit offset   (partition keeps flowing)

steps.cap: Retries use exponential backoff with jitter: two, four, eight seconds. After five failures, or immediately on a permanent error such as an invalid address, the message goes to notifications-dlq with the original payload and the error.
steps.title: Backoff, then give up
steps.code:
attempts: 2 s · 4 s · 8 s · 16 s · 32 s (± jitter)
5xx / 429 / timeout → retry
4xx invalid address → DLQ immediately, no retry
steps.note: A notification that was correctly not sent (opt-out, quiet hours, duplicate) is SUPPRESSED, not failed. It never goes to the DLQ.

steps.cap: The dead-letter queue is a daily volume, not an exception: at one percent failure that is half a million messages a day.
Admin Service consumes the DLQ, records each message in failed_alerts and raises an alarm in Slack. Developers review them in the Admin Dashboard.
steps.code:
consume notifications-dlq
INSERT INTO failed_alerts (event_id, user_id, error)
POST https://slack.com/api/chat.postMessage
  '#notif-ops: 512 311 failed, sendgrid 503'

steps.cap: When the provider recovers, someone presses Replay. Admin Service publishes the failed messages back into the main topic in batches at a configurable rate, through dedup again, skipping anything past its expires_at, so yesterday's OTP is never sent today.
steps.say: When the provider recovers, someone presses Replay. Admin Service publishes the failed messages back into the main topic in batches at a configurable rate, through dedup again, skipping anything past its expires at, so yesterday's O T P is never sent today.
steps.code:
replay 512 311 → batches of 1 000 at 200 / s
skip if expires_at < NOW()
produce notifications-bulk { ...original payload }
→ dedup SET NX again → workers
steps.note: 'Replay all' at full speed would be a self-inflicted DDoS on the provider.

recap.title: What to say in the interview

items.text: Outbox: alert + event in one transaction, 202 in milliseconds
items.cap: To sum up. The outbox commits the alert and the event together and returns 202 in milliseconds.
items.say: To sum up. The outbox commits the alert and the event together and returns two-oh-two in milliseconds.

items.text: Priority topics: critical never waits behind bulk
items.cap: Separate critical and bulk topics, with separate workers and provider quotas, so a login code never waits behind a campaign.

items.text: Idempotent at every hop: Redis SET NX + provider dedup key
items.cap: Exactly-once does not exist, so every hop is idempotent: a Redis SET NX key and a dedup key at the provider.
items.say: Exactly-once does not exist, so every hop is idempotent: a Redis set N X key and a dedup key at the provider.

items.text: Retry topic → DLQ → Replay, with backoff and expiry
items.cap: Retries go to their own topic, failures to a dead-letter queue, and replay runs through dedup and expiry at a controlled rate.

items.text: Webhooks are the real status: delivered, bounced, unsubscribed
items.cap: And the provider's 200 means accepted, not delivered. The webhooks are the real status.
items.say: And the provider's two hundred means accepted, not delivered. The webhooks are the real status.
